questions.q: The probability that a randomly chosen one-one function from the set \left\{a, b, c, d\right\}$~to the set  \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\right\}$~satisfied~$f\left(a\right) + 2f\left(b\right) - f\left(c\right) = f\left(d\right)& is$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Total& cases& will be & ${}^{5}{C}_{4} \times 4 !$

Now favourable cases for $2f \left(b\right) = f \left($c\right) + f \left(d\right) - f\left(a\right)$~will be,

Case~(I) if~$f \left(b\right) = 1$~then $f\left(c\right), f\left(d\right), f\left(a\right)$ can~take the value $3, 4, 5$~&~$4, 3, 5$~respectively

Case~(II) if $f \left(b\right) = 2$~then~$f\left(c\right), f\left(d\right), f\left(a\right)$~can take value $3, 5, 4 \text{ and } 5, 3, 4$~respectively

Case~(III) if $f \left($b\right) = 3$~then f\left($c\right), $f\left($d\right), $f\left($a\right)$~can~take value $2, 5, 1 \text{ and } 5, 2, 1$~respectively

So~total favourable case will be~$6$

So probability$= \dfrac{favourablecases}{totaloutcomes}= \dfrac{6}{5 \times 4 !} = \dfrac{1}{20}$

questions.q: Two cards are drawn successively with replacement from a well-shuffled deck of $52$ cards. Let $X$ denote the random variable of number of aces obtained in the two drawn cards. Then $P \left(X = 1\right) + P  \left($X = 2\right)$ equals:$

questions.q: Let $A$ and $B$, be two events such that the probability that exactly one of them occurs is $\dfrac{2}{5}$, and the probability that $A$ or $B$, occurs is $\dfrac{1}{2}$, then the probability of both of them occur together is.

questions.solution:
$P$ (exactly one) $= \dfrac{2}{5}$
$= P \left(A\right) + P \left($B\right) - 2P \left(A ∩ B\right) = \dfrac{2}{5} . . . \left(1\right)$
$P\left(A ∪ B\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$= P \left(A\right) + P \left(B\right) - P \left($A ∩ B\right) = $\dfrac{1}{2} . . . \left($2\right)$
$∴ $P\left($A ∩ B\right) = $\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{5 - 4}{10} = \dfrac{1}{10}.

questions.q: In a binomial distribution $B ( n, p )$, the sum and product of the mean & variance are $5$ and $6$ respectively, then find $6 ( n + p - q )$ is equal to :-
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
For the binomial distribution& $B ( n, p )$,

Mean~$= np$~and Variance~$= npq$

Sum of mean and variance~$= np + npq = 5$

$⇒ np ( 1 + q ) = 5$

$⇒ n^{2}p^{2} ( 1 + q{)}^{2} = 25$~ ~ ~....(1)

Product of~mean and variance~$= np . npq = 6$

$⇒ n^{2}p^{2}q = 6$~ ~ ~ ....(2)

Put the value of~$n^{2}p^{2}$~from equation (2) into equation (1):

$\dfrac{6}{q} ( 1 + q{)}^{2} = 25$

$⇒ 6q^{2} + 12q + 6 = 25q$

$⇒ 6q^{2} - 13q + 6 = 0$

$⇒ ( 3q - 2 ) ( 2q - 3 ) = 0$

$⇒ q = \dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{3}{2}$~where~$q = \dfrac{2}{3}$~accepted

$∴ p = \dfrac{1}{3} ⇒ n \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} + n \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} = 5$

$⇒ \dfrac{3n + 2n}{9} = 5$

$⇒ n = 9$

Therefore,

$6 ( n + p - q ) = 6\left(9 + \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}\right) = 52$

questions.q: A biased die is marked with numbers $2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 32$~on its faces and the probability of getting a face with mark~$n$ is $\dfrac{1}{n}$. If the die is thrown thrice, then the probability, that the sum of the numbers obtained is $48$, is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$P\left(2\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}, P\left(4\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}, P\left(8\right) = \dfrac{1}{8}, P\left(16\right) = \dfrac{1}{16}, P\left(32\right) = \dfrac{1}{32}$

When we get the faces as $8, 8, 32$~then the probability will be $3\left(\dfrac{1}{8} \times \dfrac{1}{8} \times \dfrac{2}{32}\right) = \dfrac{3}{1024}$

When we get the faces as $16, 16, 16$~then the probability will be $\dfrac{1}{16} \times \dfrac{1}{16} \times \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{1}{4096}$

Hence, the required probability~will be$\dfrac{3}{1024} + \dfrac{1}{4096} = \dfrac{13}{4096}$

questions.q: The probability that a randomly chosen $5$- digit number is made from exactly two digits is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Total number of five-digit numbers are& $9 \left({10}^{4}\right).

Case I :~Choosing~two non-zero digits i.e. in~$C2 9$~ways.

So, number of five-digit numbers containing both digits~$= {2}^{5} - 2$.

Case II :~Choose one non-zero and~one zero as digit i.e. in~$C1 9$~ways.

So, number of five-digit numbers containing one non-zero and one zero both~$= {2}^{4} - 1$.

So, favourable number of ways~$= C2 9 \left({2}^{5} -$2\right) + C1 9 \left({2}^{4} -$1\right) = 36\left($30\right) + 9\left($15\right) = 1080 + 135 = 1215$

Thus, required probability~$= \dfrac{1215}{9 \times {10}^{4}} = \dfrac{135}{104}.$

$

vegetarian.

option \left(4\right)$

questions.q: Suppose that $20$ pillars of the same height have been erected along the boundary of circular stadium. If the top of each pillar has been connected by beams with the top of all its non-adjacent pillars, then the total number of beams is:

Each of the beams connects& the top of two non-adjacent pillars, hence we have to find in how many ways we can select the required two pillars which are non-adjacent out of the given& $20$~pillars.

As,~$C2 20$~is the~number of beams connecting any two pillars whereas~$20$~is the number of~adjacent beams.

Thus, the total number of beams~$= C2 20 - 20$

Using~$Cr n = \dfrac{n !}{r ! \left(n - r\right) !},$

$= \dfrac{20 !}{2 ! \times 18 !} - 20$

$= \dfrac{20 \times 19 \times 18 !}{2 ! \times 18 !} - 20$

$= 190 - 20$

$= 170 .$

questions.q: A bag contains six balls of different colours. Two balls are drawn in succession with replacement. The probability that both the balls are of the same colour is $p$. Next four balls are drawn in succession with replacement and the probability that exactly three balls are of the same colours is $q$. If $p: q = m$ $: n$, where $m$ and $n$ are co-prime, then $m + n$ is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

A bag contains six balls of different colours, two balls are drawn in succession with replacement,

The probability that both the balls are of the same colour will be $p = \dfrac{6}{36}$

Now Next four balls are drawn in succession with replacement and the probability that exactly three balls are of the same colours is $q$,

So, probability will be $q = \dfrac{C1 6 \times C1 5 \times C1 4}{{6}^{4}} = \dfrac{120}{1296} = \dfrac{5}{54}$

Now the ratio of $p \text{ and } q$ will be $\dfrac{p}{q} = \dfrac{9}{5}$

Now, on comparing with $\dfrac{p}{q} = \dfrac{m}{n} ⇒ m + n = 14$
